lead: Sun exposure for acne is the practice of tanning or sitting in sunlight to make blemishes look drier, less red and less noticeable. A tan evens out skin tone, so spots can appear to recede, and community members sometimes report a short-term improvement in how their skin looks [3][4].

General acne references state that sunlight exposure is not associated with acne overall, that intense UVA can trigger a separate eruption called acne aestivalis, and that sun exposure can prolong postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, for which daily sunscreen is advised [1]. A clinic study of 400 women in Iran found that longer self-reported sun exposure was an independent predictor of post-acne pigmentation [2].

People who discuss the topic on forums are divided: some say sun seems to help back and body acne, while others say a tan only masks spots and may worsen them over time [3][4]. Dermatology uses controlled ultraviolet and blue-light phototherapy for several skin conditions, which is a separate practice from sunbathing or tanning beds [7][8].

angle.text: Users tan or sunbathe so that blemishes look less red and obvious against darker, evener skin. The change in appearance is described as short-term.

UV radiation is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen [7]

paras: Proponents say sun makes spots look drier and less inflamed for a time. A poster in a T Nation thread on back acne wrote that sun exposure seems to help, alongside washing and benzoyl peroxide [3]. Another poster in a T Nation acne thread argued that sun burns the epidermis and the evened-out skin only gives the impression that acne has receded [4]. A poster in an older thread on a bodybuilding diet suggested that excessive sun exposure combined with a high-fat diet had supposedly been tied to pimples on the back and shoulders, while noting that the matter was unsettled [9].
Wikipedia reports that sunlight is not generally associated with acne [1]. Reasons people tan include that tanned skin is often seen as healthier and can hide blemishes such as acne [7].

Acne aestivalis is a polymorphous light eruption triggered by intense UVA, including artificial UV. It usually appears one to three days after exposure on the upper arms, shoulders, back and chest and spares the face [1]. Studies cited by Wikipedia show that topical antioxidants combined with broad-spectrum sunscreen can prevent both polymorphous light eruption and acne aestivalis outbreaks [1].

Some common acne treatments increase sensitivity to sunlight: benzoyl peroxide raises photosensitivity, so sunscreen is advised during treatment, and retinoids are typically used at night for the same reason [1]. Some medications increase sensitivity to UV and burn risk more generally [7].

After an inflamed lesion heals, the skin can darken as inflammation stimulates melanocytes. Even minimal sun exposure can sustain the darkening, and daily SPF 15 or higher sunscreen can reduce the risk; untreated pigmentation can last months or years and is more common in people with darker skin [1]. Wikipedia's article on postinflammatory hyperpigmentation says UV exposure and sunburn contribute to development, darkening and spread of pigmented lesions and that it usually fades within 6 to 12 months untreated [5]. Retinoids improve it faster, and agents such as azelaic acid and arbutin may be used [1].

Dermatologists use controlled light for some skin conditions. Narrowband UVB at about 311 to 313 nm is the most common form for conditions such as psoriasis, whereas tanning beds mostly emit UVA with only 4 to 10 percent in the UVB range [8]. For acne the evidence is weaker: as of 2012, a review found evidence for light therapy and lasers not sufficient to recommend them, with moderate support for blue and blue-red light in mild acne from mostly low-quality studies and short-term benefit [8]. Wikipedia's acne article describes light and laser therapies as add-on options because of cost and limited evidence, and the benefit of blue light as unclear [1].

Wikipedia's indoor tanning article notes that tanning beds are sometimes used when clinic phototherapy is unavailable for conditions including acne and psoriasis, and that a 2015 review suggested clinicians consider them as a source of UV [7]. The history of light treatment goes back to Niels Finsen, who received the Nobel Prize in 1903 for treating lupus vulgaris with light [8].

The World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. A 2012 meta-analysis found about 20 percent higher melanoma risk among people who had ever used a tanning device and about 59 percent higher among those who began before age 35 [7]. Other documented effects include skin ageing and eye damage, and in US surveys 58 percent of indoor tanners reported burns [7]. Several countries restrict tanning beds: France banned minors in 1997, Brazil banned cosmetic use in 2009, and Australia banned commercial tanning in 2015 [7].

No studies found specifically testing tanning as an acne treatment. A 2008 comparative study in Ardabil, Iran, of 400 women (200 with melasma and acne, 200 with acne alone) found post-acne pigmentation in 45.5% overall, 66.8% with melasma against 24.1% without; longer average sun exposure and higher melanin score independently predicted higher odds of post-acne pigmentation [2][6].

timeline.event: Niels Finsen receives the Nobel Prize for light treatment of lupus vulgaris, a founding moment of phototherapy [8].
France becomes the first country to ban minors from indoor tanning [7].
A meta-analysis reports about 20 percent higher melanoma risk among people who have used tanning devices [7].

lore.intro: Sun and acne come up in bodybuilding and skin-care forums, where users compare experiences with back and body acne [3][4][9].

claims.claim: Sun exposure dries out and improves acne.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster reported that sun exposure seems to help back acne [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia states sunlight is not generally associated with acne overall and that sun can prolong post-acne pigmentation [1][5]. Controlled phototherapy has its own evidence base, which is weaker for acne than for psoriasis [8].

claims.claim: A tan only masks acne and may worsen it.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said a tan evens out the skin and gives a false impression that acne has receded, and that sun ages the skin faster [4].
claims.experts: UV is documented to darken and spread post-inflammatory pigmentation, and intense UVA can trigger acne aestivalis [1][5].

claims.claim: Tanning beds can stand in for dermatology light therapy.
claims.believers: Users sometimes reach for tanning beds as a convenient source of UV for skin conditions.
claims.experts: A 2015 review suggested clinicians consider tanning beds when clinic phototherapy is unavailable, but beds emit mostly UVA, may treat psoriasis less effectively than UVB, and carry cancer risks [7][8].

name: Sun exposure for acne

card.summary: Tanning to dry out spots; reference sources link sun to lingering dark marks rather than clearer skin.
card.note: Sun can prolong post-acne pigmentation per general references.

quick.overview:
Some people tan or sunbathe in the hope of drying out acne. The effect, when reported, is described as temporary.

General references say sunlight is not associated with acne overall but can sustain post-acne dark marks.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say UV makes blemishes look drier and less red; no published trial supports it as a treatment.
quick.risks: UV can sustain postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, and intense UVA can trigger acne aestivalis; sunscreen is advised by references.
